## 0001 — Postgres with pgvector as the only datastore

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** The system needs dense vector search and a keyword/BM25-style
retriever so that hybrid retrieval can be ablated against each one alone.

**Options.**
- A dedicated vector database (Qdrant, Weaviate) plus Elasticsearch or OpenSearch.
- Postgres 16 with `pgvector` for dense search and built-in full-text search
  (`tsvector` + GIN) for keyword search.

**Choice.** Postgres with pgvector, both retrievers in one database.

**Why.** Two engines mean two deployments, two backup stories and two sets of
consistency problems, for a corpus measured in thousands of chunks rather than
hundreds of millions. One database also makes hybrid fusion a single SQL round
trip and keeps the AWS footprint in Phase 6 to one RDS instance. Postgres FTS is
not literally BM25 — `ts_rank_cd` is a different ranking function — and the
evaluation write-up must say so rather than calling it BM25.

---

## 0002 — A shared `schemas/` package

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** `Chunk`, `RetrievedChunk` and `Citation` are needed by `ingest`,
`index`, `retrieve`, `generate` and `eval` alike.

**Options.**
- Define each model in the package that first needs it and import across packages.
- One `schemas/` package that every other package imports from.

**Choice.** A shared `schemas/` package.

**Why.** The first option produces import cycles as soon as `eval` needs both a
`Chunk` and a `RetrievedChunk` — by Phase 4 the dependency graph is a knot. A
leaf package that imports nothing from its siblings keeps the graph acyclic by
construction. The cost is one extra package in the tree.

---

## 0003 — Plain SQL migrations instead of Alembic

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** The schema needs versioned, repeatable migrations, including
pgvector-specific DDL (HNSW index options) that ORMs model poorly.

**Options.**
- Alembic, which means adding SQLAlchemy to a project with no ORM.
- Numbered `.sql` files applied in order by a small runner that records applied
  versions in a `schema_migrations` table.

**Choice.** Numbered SQL files plus a runner.

**Why.** Alembic's value is autogenerating diffs from ORM models, and there are
no ORM models here — queries are hand-written SQL so that hybrid retrieval and
RRF stay explicit and tunable. Adding SQLAlchemy purely to drive migrations is a
large dependency for little gain, and `CREATE INDEX ... USING hnsw (...) WITH
(m = ..., ef_construction = ...)` would be raw SQL inside Alembic anyway. The
runner is roughly thirty lines. Revisit if the schema outgrows forward-only
migrations.

---

## 0004 — Pin Python to 3.12

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** The brief allows 3.11 or newer; the development machine has 3.12.10.

**Options.** Support 3.11+ broadly, or pin a single version matched by CI.

**Choice.** `requires-python = ">=3.12,<3.13"`, and CI resolves the same version.

**Why.** A reproducibility project should not have local and CI resolving
different dependency trees — a lockfile only pins packages, not the interpreter
that determines which wheels those packages resolve to. 3.12 is what is already
installed, and nothing in the stack needs 3.11 compatibility. Widening the range
later is cheap; debugging a 3.11-only CI failure is not.

---

## 0005 — Heavy ML dependencies behind an optional extra

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** `sentence-transformers` pulls in `torch`, roughly 2.5 GB on
Windows. It is needed for embedding and reranking, and for nothing else.

**Options.**
- One dependency list, so every `uv sync` and every CI run installs torch.
- A `[project.optional-dependencies] ml` extra installed with `uv sync --extra ml`.

**Choice.** The optional extra.

**Why.** Lint, type-check and unit tests never touch a model. Installing torch
on every CI run would add minutes to every push for no coverage. Everything is
still declared in `pyproject.toml`, so nothing is hidden and the full
environment is one flag away. The Phase 5 CI eval gate runs retrieval-only
against a committed index snapshot and so will need this extra — the workflow
will opt in explicitly at that point.

---

## 0006 — No CLI framework

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** Phases 1–4 need command-line entry points for ingest, query, serve
and eval.

**Options.** Add Typer or Click, or use `python -m rbi_rag.<package>` with
`argparse` behind `poe` tasks.

**Choice.** `python -m` plus `argparse`.

**Why.** `poe` already provides task discovery and help text, which is most of
what a CLI framework is bought for. The commands take a handful of flags each.
Rule 8 says not to add dependencies outside the agreed stack without asking, and
this one would not earn its place.

---

## 0007 — Unimplemented tasks fail loudly

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 0

**Context.** Phase 0 defines `poe` tasks for `ingest`, `query`, `serve` and
`eval`, none of which exist yet.

**Options.** Omit the tasks until their phase lands; have them print a notice
and exit 0; have them exit non-zero.

**Choice.** Exit with status 2 and a message naming the phase.

**Why.** The brief asks for the tasks in Phase 0, so omitting them is out. A
zero exit is worse than useless: it would let a broken pipeline pass a CI step
or a scripted run while reporting success, which is the exact failure mode the
"never invent a result" rule exists to prevent. Exit 2 is unambiguous to both a
human and a shell.

## 0008 — Browser-assisted PDF acquisition

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 1

**Context.** RBI serves Master Direction PDFs from `rbidocs.rbi.org.in`, which
answers scripted clients with an F5 BIG-IP JavaScript challenge page carrying a
200 status and `Content-Type: text/html`. Measured during Phase 1 planning:
ordinary cookie handling does not satisfy it across repeated requests. The
listing host, `www.rbi.org.in`, has no such protection and serves 788 KB of
real HTML to a plain client.

**Options.**
- Solve the challenge: execute its JavaScript, or drive a headless browser.
- Use a TLS/HTTP client that imitates a browser fingerprint.
- Separate acquisition from ingestion: harvest metadata by script, obtain PDFs
  through a real browser, and process from a local raw store.
- Abandon the RBI corpus.

**Choice.** Separate acquisition from ingestion.

**Why.** The first two options defeat an access control the publisher put there
deliberately, and the fact that the documents are public does not make
circumventing it acceptable. The third gives up nothing that matters: the
manifest, the content hashing, the idempotency guarantee and every downstream
stage are unchanged, because they were always going to read from `data/raw/`.
What is lost is unattended end-to-end automation, which costs one manual step
per corpus refresh.

The seam is the `Fetcher` protocol in `ingest/fetch.py`. `LocalFetcher` reads
the raw store; `BlockedHttpFetcher` exists solely to raise with an explanation,
so the reason is discoverable from the code and not only from this file. If RBI
ever permits scripted access, one implementation replaces the other.

One guard earns its place: a browser that hits the challenge saves an HTML page
under a `.PDF` name. `looks_like_pdf` checks the magic bytes, because such a
file would otherwise parse to an empty document and silently shrink the corpus.

---

## 0009 — Treating an unreachable robots.txt as permissive

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 1

**Context.** The brief requires respecting `robots.txt`. RBI returns HTTP 418
for `https://www.rbi.org.in/robots.txt` to every scripted client tried, so its
policy cannot be read at all.

**Options.** Treat any failure as a full disallow and stop; ignore robots
entirely; or follow the status-code semantics the standard defines.

**Choice.** Follow RFC 9309 §2.3.1: a 4xx means no policy is published and
access is unrestricted; a 5xx or a network failure means assume a complete
disallow. 418 is a 4xx, so harvesting proceeds.

**Why.** This is the behaviour the standard specifies, not a convenience. The
important part is honesty about it: `PoliteClient.robots_decision` returns the
reason alongside the verdict, and the harvest report prints it, so every run
records that no policy was actually read rather than implying one was honoured.
The two-second floor between requests is enforced in `Settings` regardless.

---

## 0010 — Harvesting metadata from the listing page alone

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 1

**Context.** The manifest needs url, title, circular number, date and
department. The listing page carries title, date, category and the PDF link.
Each entry also links to a detail page, and RBI prints the circular number and
department on page 1 of every Master Direction.

**Options.** Fetch one detail page per Direction (~380 extra requests), or take
the identifiers off the PDF during parsing.

**Choice.** Read them from the PDF; never fetch detail pages.

**Why.** It turns 380 requests into one, which matters when the standing rate
limit is two seconds. The detail pages are also heavily JavaScript-driven,
making them a worse parsing target than the PDF's own first page. The cost is
that circular number and department are unknown until a PDF is acquired, which
is why `merge_harvested` preserves PDF-derived fields across a re-harvest
rather than letting the listing overwrite them with nulls.

---

## 0011 — Block-based PDF text extraction

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 1

**Context.** The chunker packs paragraphs up to a token budget, so it needs to
know where paragraphs end.

**Options.** PyMuPDF's flat `get_text("text")`, or `get_text("blocks")` joined
with a blank line.

**Choice.** Blocks.

**Why.** Flat extraction separates every line with a single newline and gives
no paragraph boundary at all, so an entire page collapses into one unit and
"chunking" degenerates into fixed-width slicing of a page. That would have made
the `section_aware` versus `fixed_tokens` comparison in Phase 4 meaningless,
since both arms would have been doing the same thing. Blocks correspond to
paragraphs and are already in reading order once sorted by position.

---

## 0012 — Chunking by accumulating paragraphs, not by slicing tokens

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 1

**Context.** A chunker can either tokenise the document and slice fixed windows
of token ids, decoding each back to text, or accumulate whole paragraphs until
the budget is reached.

**Options.** As above.

**Choice.** Accumulate paragraphs.

**Why.** Decoding token ids back to text is lossy: it normalises whitespace and
can alter punctuation, so the stored chunk would differ from the source it
points at. This system's entire claim is that a citation can be checked against
the PDF, and a quote that does not appear in the document breaks that claim.
A test asserts every chunk's paragraphs appear verbatim in the source text.

The cost is that chunks land under the budget rather than exactly on it, and
that an oversized paragraph needs splitting on sentences and then on words.

---

## 0013 — Adding `tokenizers` as a direct dependency

**Date:** 2026-10-29 · **Phase:** 1

**Context.** Chunk size is the independent variable of the Phase 4 ablation, so
it must be counted with the tokenizer the embedding model actually uses.
`sentence-transformers` provides one but lives behind the optional `ml` extra
(entry 0005), and pulling torch in just to count tokens would undo that.

**Options.** Approximate with a whitespace or character heuristic; require the
`ml` extra for chunking; or depend on `tokenizers` directly.

**Choice.** `tokenizers` as a base dependency, behind a `TokenCounter` Protocol.

**Why.** An approximation is not defensible when the number being approximated
*is* the variable under study. `tokenizers` is a small Rust binding with no
torch dependency, and it is already a transitive dependency of
`sentence-transformers`, so it adds nothing to the eventual full install. The
Protocol keeps tests offline: they inject `WhitespaceTokenCounter`, which warns
loudly that its counts must never be reported.

**Measured, not assumed.** The tokenizer does not enforce the model's sequence
limit: `BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5` encoded 2,000 words to 2,000 tokens with no
truncation configured. The 512-token cap belongs to the model, so a 1024-token
chunk will be truncated silently inside `sentence-transformers` at embed time.
Phase 2 must assert the model's real `max_seq_length` and refuse, or loudly
record, any chunk that exceeds it. See the note in README under Limitations.

---

## 0014 — onnxruntime as the embedding backend, not sentence-transformers

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 2

**Context.** The agreed stack names sentence-transformers, which means torch:
roughly 2.5 GB on Windows. Phase 5 runs a retrieval eval in CI on every push,
so that install cost recurs forever. Both `bge-small-en-v1.5` and
`bge-reranker-base` publish ONNX exports under an MIT licence, and
`onnxruntime` was already present in the dependency tree as a PyMuPDF
transitive dependency.

**Options.**
- sentence-transformers, as specified: the reference implementation, zero
  correctness risk, 2.5 GB.
- onnxruntime: ~130 MB, CPU-fast, but pooling and normalisation have to be
  implemented here rather than inherited.
- Both: ONNX by default, sentence-transformers retained purely to validate it.

**Choice.** The third. ONNX is the default; sentence-transformers stays in the
`ml` extra and is used by nothing except `tests/test_embed_parity.py`.

**Why.** The risk of hand-rolling pooling is real and specific: bge uses
**CLS** pooling, not mean pooling, and getting that wrong produces vectors that
look entirely plausible while retrieving worse. That is not a risk to argue
away, so it is measured instead.

**Measured.** Over the parity sentence set, against sentence-transformers:

| Quantity | Value |
| --- | --- |
| Max elementwise difference | 1.639e-07 |
| Mean elementwise difference | 3.202e-08 |
| Minimum cosine similarity | 1.00000000 |
| Dimension (ONNX / reference) | 384 / 384 |
| Content-token limit (ONNX / reference) | 510 / 510 |

That is float32 rounding, not an implementation difference. The parity suite
also asserts the two backends rank the same sentences in the same order, since
a difference too small to see could still reorder results.

The parity test is excluded from the default suite and from CI, because
installing torch on every push is the cost this decision exists to avoid. Run
it with `uv sync --extra ml` and `uv run poe test-parity` whenever the embedder
changes.

This adds three direct dependencies — `onnxruntime`, `huggingface-hub` and
`numpy` — all of which were already installed transitively, so the resolved
environment is unchanged. They are declared explicitly because depending on
another package's transitive dependencies is fragile.

## 0015 — Postgres full-text search as the keyword retriever

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 2

**Context.** The hybrid retriever needs a lexical counterpart to dense search.
The stack puts both in one database.

**Options.** A separate search engine with real BM25, or Postgres full-text
search with a GIN-indexed `tsvector`.

**Choice.** Postgres FTS: a generated `tsvector` column using the `english`
configuration, queried with `websearch_to_tsquery` and ranked by `ts_rank_cd`.

**Why.** Entry 0001 already committed to one datastore. `websearch_to_tsquery`
accepts quoted phrases and negation without throwing on input a user might
reasonably type, which `to_tsquery` does not. The column is `GENERATED ALWAYS`
so the index can never drift out of step with the text it indexes.

**The caveat that must be reported.** `ts_rank_cd` is **not BM25**. It has no
document-length normalisation of the kind BM25 applies, and no tunable k1/b.
Calling this arm "BM25" in the results would be wrong, so it is called "FTS"
everywhere. The `english` configuration also applies Snowball stemming, which
is right for ordinary prose but conflates regulatory terms a lawyer would
distinguish. If this arm underperforms, that is a candidate explanation and
should be investigated rather than reported as a dense-versus-sparse finding.

---

## 0016 — Evaluation searches exactly; HNSW serves queries

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 2

**Context.** HNSW is an approximate index: it trades recall for speed. The
Phase 4 ablation compares retrievers on recall@k.

**Options.** Measure through HNSW like production does, or measure with exact
kNN and treat the index as a serving concern.

**Choice.** `RetrievalConfig.exact` forces a sequential scan, evaluation sets
it, and HNSW-versus-exact agreement is reported as its own number.

**Why.** Running eval queries through an approximate index mixes the index's
own recall loss into the retriever comparison, where it is indistinguishable
from a real effect. With a corpus of roughly 19,000 chunks an exact scan is
cheap, so there is no reason to accept that contamination. The index still
exists and is still measured — just not as a hidden term in someone else's
result. An integration test asserts the two orderings agree on the fixture
corpus; if they ever diverge, every number measured through HNSW is suspect.

---

## 0017 — One partial HNSW index per chunk set

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 2

**Context.** The ablation sweeps chunking strategy against chunk size, so
several chunk sets live in the `chunks` table simultaneously and each query
must see exactly one of them.

**Options.** A single HNSW index over every row with a `chunk_set_id` filter,
pgvector 0.8's `hnsw.iterative_scan`, or a partial index per set.

**Choice.** A partial index per set, created by the index builder.

**Why.** A shared index forces post-filtering: HNSW returns its nearest
neighbours across all sets and the filter then discards most of them, so the
effective recall for any one set is far below what the index would give on its
own. That is the problem in entry 0016 wearing a different hat. A partial index
contains only its own set, so no filtering is needed. Six configurations means
six small indexes, which costs build time and nothing else. An integration test
asserts the index definition really is restricted to its chunk set.

---

## 0018 — Reciprocal Rank Fusion in Python, not SQL

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 2

**Context.** Hybrid retrieval fuses a dense ranking with a keyword ranking.
Both come from the same database, so the fusion could be a single SQL query.

**Options.** One SQL statement with CTEs, or two queries fused in Python.

**Choice.** Two queries, fused in `retrieve/fuse.py`.

**Why.** The Phase 2 done-criterion is that every retriever is unit-tested and
switchable purely by config. Fusion in Python is a pure function over lists of
ids: its tests need no database, no fixtures and no Postgres running, and they
can assert the property that justifies RRF at all — that a chunk both
retrievers rank beats a chunk only one of them ranks. The same logic in SQL
would only be testable through an integration test.

It also avoids inventing a normalisation. Dense scores are cosine similarities
in [-1, 1]; `ts_rank_cd` is unbounded and scaled differently. RRF uses only
rank positions, so the two never need to be made commensurable. The cost is one
extra round trip per hybrid query.

---

## 0019 — The container's Postgres listens on 5434

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 2

**Context.** Integration tests failed with `password authentication failed for
user "rbi"` while the container reported healthy and `docker compose exec psql`
worked. A locally installed PostgreSQL 18 service was listening on 5432 and
answering instead of the container. 5433 was then held by a stale Docker
binding.

**Options.** Ask the developer to stop their local Postgres, or move the
container off the contested port.

**Choice.** Default `POSTGRES_PORT` to 5434, used by both `docker-compose.yml`
and the DSN in `Settings`, so the two cannot disagree.

**Why.** A natively installed Postgres on 5432 is common on developer machines,
and this failure mode is unusually confusing: the container is healthy, the
credentials are right, and the error says the password is wrong. Stopping
someone's local database to run a side project is the wrong trade. Changing one
setting is not.

---

## 0020 — Abstention has two gates, and no invented threshold

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 3

**Context.** The brief asks the system to abstain when retrieval confidence is
low, with a configurable threshold. The setting that existed,
`abstain_threshold = 0.35`, was incoherent: the three retrievers return scores
on unrelated scales. Measured in Phase 2 on the same query — dense cosine
**0.83**, `ts_rank_cd` **0.00185**, RRF **0.03279**. One cutoff across all three
abstains on every hybrid and keyword query and never on a dense one, while
looking like a working safety feature.

**Options.** Per-retriever thresholds; normalise the scores onto a common
scale; threshold only a signal that is already comparable; or drop the
retrieval gate and rely on the model's own judgement.

**Choice.** Two independent gates.

1. A retrieval gate, compared against the **reranker score** where there is
   one and the **raw dense cosine** otherwise. Never against an RRF score. When
   neither exists — a keyword-only query — the gate does not fire, because
   there is no comparable number and `ts_rank_cd` is not one. This is why
   `dense_score` is carried on `RetrievedChunk` separately from `score`.
2. The model's own `sufficient_evidence` field, which always applies.

**Why the threshold ships as `None`.** Picking a number now would mean
reporting a threshold nobody measured, which rule 1 forbids. Phase 4 produces
labelled unanswerable questions; that is the first point at which a defensible
value exists. Until then gate 2 does the work, and gate 1 is plumbing waiting
for its number.

---

## 0021 — Citations are validated at the quote, and the pipeline fails closed

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 3

**Context.** The brief requires that every cited chunk be in the retrieved set.
That check alone is weaker than it sounds: a model can attach a fluent,
confident, entirely invented sentence to a chunk_id it really was shown, and an
id-only check passes it.

**Options.** Check ids only; check ids and quotes; or check quotes with fuzzy
matching to tolerate near-misses.

**Choice.** Both checks, with exact matching after whitespace normalisation,
and failure closes the door: one retry with the violations fed back, then
abstention.

**Why.** Whitespace normalisation forgives line wrapping, which is an artifact
of PDF rendering and not a different quote. Nothing else is forgiven — no case
folding, no punctuation stripping, no fuzzy similarity — because a quote that
differs by a word is a different claim, and a system whose entire value is
verifiability cannot ship "close enough". Quotes under 12 characters are
rejected: a fragment that short appears everywhere and evidences nothing.

Two further rules follow from the same reasoning. An answer that passes
validation but cites **nothing** is treated as a failure, since an uncited
claim is unverifiable however plausible it reads. And when retries are
exhausted the system abstains rather than returning the answer with the bad
citations stripped — stripping would leave a confident answer whose support had
just been shown to be fabricated.

---

## 0022 — Structured output through `messages.parse`, not prefill or forced tools

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 3

**Context.** The answer, its citations and its abstention flag have to come
back as parseable structure, not prose to be regexed.

**Options.** Assistant prefill to open a JSON object; a forced `tool_choice` so
the model must call a schema-shaped tool; or the structured-output API.

**Choice.** `client.messages.parse(output_format=AnswerPayload)` with
`output_config`.

**Why.** The first two are the familiar tricks and both now return **400** on
current models: assistant prefill is rejected, and forced `tool_choice`
(`any`/`tool`) is rejected on Claude Sonnet 5.5. Structured outputs is the
supported path and validates the response against the Pydantic model, which is
what we wanted anyway.

Three related constraints are recorded in `generate/client.py` because each is
a 400 if got wrong: thinking cannot be disabled on this model (depth is set
with `output_config.effort`), thinking tokens count against `max_tokens`, and
`temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k` were removed API-wide.

---

## 0023 — Costs come from a dated table, and unknown models cost `None`

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 3

**Context.** `/query` reports `cost_usd`. Prices change, and a figure computed
from a stale table is wrong without saying so.

**Options.** Hard-code prices inline; put them in settings; or keep a table
that carries its own date.

**Choice.** A table in `generate/cost.py` with `PRICE_TABLE_DATE`, surfaced on
`/health`. A model with no entry yields `None`, never an estimate.

**Why.** Prices are reference data about the world, not per-deployment
configuration, so settings is the wrong home. The date is the point: it makes
staleness visible instead of letting an old number flow into the Phase 4 cost
column as though it were current. Returning `None` for an unpriced model is the
same rule as everywhere else in this project — no number appears unless
something measured it. Cached reads and cache writes are billed at their own
rates rather than folded into input tokens, a difference of an order of
magnitude.

---

## 0024 — Claude Sonnet 5.5 as the default model

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 3

**Context.** Anthropic's current guidance is to default to `claude-opus-5-5`
and to treat choosing a cheaper model as the user's decision. Phase 4 runs an
LLM-as-judge over every eval item, so the model choice is multiplied by the
size of the eval set.

**Options.** `claude-opus-5-5` at $4/$20 per MTok, or `claude-sonnet-5-5` at
$2/$10.

**Choice.** `claude-sonnet-5-5`, chosen by the repository owner.

**Why.** Roughly half the cost on a workload — answering from supplied
excerpts — that is extraction and synthesis rather than open-ended reasoning.
`ANTHROPIC_MODEL` overrides it per run, so answering and judging can use
different models, and Phase 4 should report which model produced which numbers
rather than leaving it implicit.

`ANTHROPIC_EFFORT` defaults to `medium` and is **untuned**. The model's own
default is `high`, which is calibrated for agentic and coding work; answering
from supplied context is neither. Phase 4 should sweep it rather than leaving
it to taste.

---

## 0025 — The API starts degraded rather than refusing to boot

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 3

**Context.** The application needs an Anthropic key, a database and local model
files. Any of them can be missing in a fresh checkout or a bad deployment.

**Options.** Fail startup on the first missing dependency, or start and report
health per dependency.

**Choice.** Start. `/health` returns 200 with `status: degraded` and a
per-dependency breakdown; `/query` returns 503 until the gap is closed.

**Why.** A process that exits during startup leaves its reason in a log nobody
is reading yet; a running `/health` endpoint answers "what is missing" directly.
The breakdown is per dependency on purpose — a monitor needs to know *which*
one is down, not merely that something is.

**A bug this found.** `.env.example` ships `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=` with no value,
and pydantic read that as `SecretStr("")` — not `None`. `/health` therefore
reported `api_key_configured: true` with no key present, and the failure would
have surfaced as an authentication error on a user's first real query. Settings
now treats a blank or whitespace key as absent, with tests covering both.

---

## 0026 — Gold evidence is labelled as spans, not as chunk ids

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 4

**Context.** The brief specifies `gold_chunk_ids` on each eval item. A chunk id
encodes its chunking configuration (`{doc_id}-{strategy}-{size}-{index}-{hash}`),
and the ablation compares six configurations.

**Measured.** Chunking one fixture document four ways and intersecting the id
sets:

```
('fixed_tokens', 20) vs ('fixed_tokens', 40):   0 shared
('fixed_tokens', 20) vs ('section_aware', 20):  0 shared
('section_aware', 20) vs ('section_aware', 40): 0 shared
          ... every pair: 0 shared
```

**Options.** Label gold chunk ids per configuration (six times the work, and
six incomparable gold sets); label once against one configuration and accept
that five arms are unmeasurable; or label at a level the chunker cannot move.

**Choice.** `GoldSpan(doc_id, page_start, page_end, quote)`. A chunk covers a
span when it is from that document, its page range overlaps, and — where a
quote is given — it contains that quote.

**Why.** Following the brief literally would have produced a gold set valid for
exactly one arm of the grid and empty for the other five, so the headline
comparison of the whole project could not have been computed. Document, page
and quote are properties of the source PDF, so one label serves every arm, and
re-chunking never invalidates the eval set.

The quote matters as much as the pages: page overlap alone is generous on a
dense page, and a 1024-token chunk would otherwise "cover" a span it merely
sits near. `resolve_gold_chunk_ids` still derives the ids for a given chunk set,
so a result stays inspectable — but as output, never as a label.

---

## 0027 — Retrieval metrics count spans found, not chunks retrieved

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 4

**Context.** With gold spans in place, recall@k could still be computed the
conventional way: relevant chunks retrieved divided by relevant chunks total.

**Options.** Chunk-counting recall, or span-covering recall.

**Choice.** Recall@k is the fraction of gold **spans** covered by at least one
chunk in the top k. MRR uses the first chunk covering any span. nDCG awards
gain only where a chunk is the *first* to cover a span.

**Why.** The number of chunks covering a fixed piece of evidence falls as chunk
size rises. Under chunk-counting recall, a 1024-token configuration needs to
find two chunks where a 256-token one needs eight, so it scores higher for
reasons that have nothing to do with retrieval quality — the exact confound
that would make "bigger chunks are better" the headline finding. Counting spans
asks the question that matters: was the evidence surfaced in the top k?

The nDCG novelty rule closes the mirror-image loophole: without it, a
configuration that splits one span across many small chunks is rewarded for
returning the same evidence repeatedly. A test asserts both chunkings of the
same document score identically, and a companion test shows the chunk counts
genuinely differ — so the property is demonstrated, not asserted.

---

## 0028 — Full grid for retrieval, a derived subset for generation

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 4

**Context.** The grid is 3 chunk sizes × 2 strategies × 3 retrievers × 2 rerank
settings = 36 arms. Retrieval costs nothing. Generation costs an answer call
and a judge call per item per arm.

**Estimated** from the committed price table at `claude-sonnet-5-5`, assuming
~5,500 input tokens per answer and 2.5× output for thinking:

| Questions | Full grid | 6-arm subset |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 30 | ~$59 | ~$10 |
| 50 | ~$99 | ~$17 |
| 100 | ~$198 | ~$33 |

**Choice.** Retrieval across all 36 arms; generation on a subset, chosen by the
repository owner at six arms.

**Why.** Generation quality is largely downstream of retrieval, so 36 arms of
answering pays roughly six times over for what the retrieval table already
shows. The subset is **derived from the retrieval results**, not hand-picked:
the best arm on recall@5, the other retrievers at that chunk configuration, and
the rerank toggle. That makes the choice reproducible and makes each included
arm answer a question rather than sample the space. `--arms N` widens it.

Those dollar figures are estimates with stated assumptions. The measured cost
goes into `results/generation.md` from real usage.

---

## 0029 — Faithfulness is reported with its calibration, or as TODO

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 4

**Context.** Faithfulness is scored by an LLM judge. Most answers in a working
system are faithful, so a judge that always answered "faithful" would score
around 90% raw agreement with a human and be worthless.

**Options.** Report faithfulness alone; report it with raw agreement; report it
with a chance-corrected statistic.

**Choice.** Cohen's kappa against the owner's labels on a subset, printed next
to the faithfulness score. With no human labels the report says
`judge calibration: TODO` rather than printing an unqualified number.

**Why.** Raw agreement is exactly the statistic a lazy judge games; kappa near
zero exposes it, and a test pins that down — a judge that says "faithful" nine
times out of ten against a human who disagrees once scores kappa 0.0. A
constant labeller on either side is flagged as degenerate in the output,
because kappa is not meaningful there and a reader should not take 1.0 at face
value.

The judge's prompt is scoped to support, not correctness: a claim true of
Indian banking regulation but absent from the cited excerpts is unsupported.
Otherwise the metric quietly becomes a test of the judge's own knowledge.

---

## 0030 — Generation results are cached, and are not deterministic

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 4

**Context.** The Phase 4 done-criterion is that `uv run poe eval` reproduces
the results tables from a clean run. An LLM is not deterministic.

**Options.** Claim reproducibility and quietly not have it; pin a seed the API
does not offer; or cache responses and state plainly what reproduces.

**Choice.** Cache by content hash — model, prompt, retrieved context, answer —
and say in the results header that retrieval tables reproduce exactly while
generation tables replay from cache and re-sample when the cache is cleared.

**Why.** The alternative is a reproducibility claim that fails the first time
someone checks it. The cache key covers everything that could change a
response, so a changed prompt or a different arm re-runs rather than serving a
verdict about different text. `--no-cache` forces a fresh sample.

---

## 0031 — Postgres full-text search matches disjunctively

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 4

**Context.** The FTS retriever used `websearch_to_tsquery`, which builds a
**conjunctive** query. Running the ablation against the real database, every
FTS arm scored 0.0 recall on a question whose answer was indexed:

```
tsquery: 'minimum' & 'capit' & 'ratio' & 'must' & 'bank' & 'maintain'
per-chunk match: all False
match on 'capital ratio': page 2, page 3    <- the text was right there
```

The passage does not contain "must", so the conjunction failed.

**Options.** Keep conjunctive matching and report the result; strip question
words with a stopword list of our own; or match disjunctively and rank.

**Choice.** Build the tsquery as a disjunction of the query's own lexemes,
taken from Postgres's tokenizer, and let `ts_rank_cd` discriminate.

**Why.** Reporting the conjunctive result would have published "FTS recall@5 =
0.00" as a finding about keyword retrieval when it was a bug in the query
builder — a confidently wrong headline in exactly the comparison this project
exists to make. Lexical retrieval is disjunctive and ranked; BM25 is too.
Hand-rolling a stopword list would be guessing at which question words to drop.

The cost is that explicit operators (quoted phrases, negation) are no longer
honoured by this retriever. For natural-language questions that is far the
smaller loss, and it is documented.

**How it hid.** The in-memory store used by unit tests scored by term overlap —
disjunctive — while Postgres was conjunctive. The fake and the real thing
disagreed on semantics, so the unit tests passed throughout. Both are
disjunctive now, and the docstring says to keep them agreeing: a fake that
behaves differently from the system is not evidence about the system.

---

## 0032 — The CI gate is a canary, not a quality measure

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 5

**Context.** CI needs a cheap, deterministic retrieval check on every push. The
real evaluation needs a downloaded corpus and a human-verified question set,
neither of which belongs in a per-push job.

**Options.** Gate on the real eval set (needs the corpus in CI, or rebuilt
there); gate on a committed fixture snapshot; or skip the gate.

**Choice.** A committed fixture snapshot under `eval/snapshot/`, with its own
fixture questions, and vocabulary that keeps it separate from measurement.

**Why.** The gate answers "did retrieval change since the baseline was
recorded", which is worth blocking a merge over. It does not answer "is
retrieval good", and its numbers must never appear in README or `results/`.
The distinction is stated in the gate's own output, in the module docstring and
in CLAUDE.md, because a recall figure pulled out of a CI log a year from now
will otherwise get quoted as a project result.

This also keeps rule 2 intact. The fixture questions are a tripwire over a
fixture PDF, not claims about RBI, so they carry `verified_by_human=false` and
the gate never filters on that flag. Nothing about this path can turn generated
questions into reported ground truth.

**Three sub-decisions.**

*Committed query vectors.* `PrecomputedEmbedder` replays vectors stored
alongside the chunk vectors, satisfying the Embedder protocol so the whole
retrieval stack runs unchanged. CI needs no model download and no network, so
the gate cannot flake on a HuggingFace rate limit — and a flaky gate gets
ignored, which is worse than a narrow one. The cost is real: a regression
inside `OnnxEmbedder` will not trip the gate. `poe test-model` covers that
separately. The manifest records the model and dimension, and loading fails
loudly when `Settings` has moved, because silently scoring an old model's
vectors would make the gate worse than useless.

*Real Postgres, not the in-memory store.* The fake would have been faster and
needed no service container. It also scores keyword search by term overlap
while Postgres uses `ts_rank_cd` — the exact divergence that let a completely
broken FTS retriever pass the entire unit suite in Phase 4. A gate that
measures the fake measures the wrong thing.

*Snapshot size.* 33 KB for the fixture: `.npy` float32 rather than JSON, which
would have been roughly five times larger. A realistic 200-chunk snapshot is
about 300 KB.

---

## 0033 — The gate checks order-sensitive metrics, not recall@5 alone

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 5

**Context.** The brief specifies that CI "fails if recall@5 drops more than a
configurable threshold". Built exactly that way, the gate was then tested by
inverting the dense retriever — ranking by *furthest* vector instead of
nearest.

**Measured.** The gate passed, exit code 0:

```
  ok   section_aware-512-dense-norerank recall@5: 1.0000 vs baseline 1.0000 (+0.0000)
PASSED: nothing regressed.
```

The same broken retriever, measured across more metrics:

| metric | broken | healthy |
| --- | --- | --- |
| recall@5 | **1.0000** | 1.0000 |
| recall@1 | 0.0000 | 1.0000 |
| MRR | 0.2500 | 1.0000 |
| nDCG@5 | 0.4307 | 1.0000 |

**Why it happened.** The fixture snapshot holds 4 chunks and k runs up to 10.
When the corpus is smaller than k, every chunk is retrieved whatever the
ranking, so recall@k is pinned at 1.0 and cannot move. Recall measures
*whether* the evidence came back; it says nothing about *where* in the list.

**Choice.** `EVAL_GATE_METRICS` defaults to `recall@1`, `recall@5`, `mrr`, and
any of them dropping past the tolerance fails the build. The gate also prints a
warning when the snapshot holds fewer chunks than the largest k, naming the
limitation rather than leaving it to be discovered.

**Why not just enlarge the corpus.** A bigger snapshot helps and should happen
once real documents exist, but it does not fix the underlying point: recall@k
is insensitive to ordering by construction, and a retriever can degrade badly
while still returning the right chunk somewhere in the top k. The order-
sensitive metrics are what make the gate bite.

**Verified.** With the fix in place and the retriever inverted again, the gate
fails with exit code 1 on `recall@1` and `mrr` for dense and hybrid, leaves FTS
untouched (it does not use vectors), and `recall@5` still reads 1.0000 on every
row — the brief's metric passing a broken retriever, visible in the output.

This is a deliberate extension of the brief. Implemented literally, the gate
would have been green for as long as the project lived.

---

## 0034 — The reranker stays out of the image, and off by default

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 6

**Context.** Instance sizing needed a real number, so the running process was
measured rather than estimated:

```
baseline python              :    19.8 MB
+ project imports            :    55.0 MB
+ embedder loaded & warmed   :   241.7 MB   (+186.7)
+ reranker loaded & warmed   :  1562.5 MB   (+1320.8)

BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5         126.9 MB on disk
BAAI/bge-reranker-base        1060.9 MB on disk
```

The reranker costs **1.32 GB of RAM and 1.06 GB of image**. I checked whether
that was onnxruntime's memory arena rather than the model, and it is not — the
exported file really is a gigabyte.

**Options.** Bake both models in and size the host for 2 GiB; bake neither in
and download at first use; or bake in the embedder and leave the reranker
optional.

**Choice.** The embedder is baked into the image; the reranker is not, and
`RERANK_ENABLED` defaults to false.

**Why.** The embedder is on every request path, so a cold start that reaches
HuggingFace would be slow, rate-limitable, and fatal in a subnet with no
egress — the image sets `HF_HUB_OFFLINE=1` so this is verified at build time
rather than discovered in production.

The reranker is the difference between a free-tier `t3.micro` and a `t3.small`
at roughly $15/month. And the argument against paying is not really about
money: **Phase 4's ablation has not run**, so nobody knows yet whether
reranking improves anything on this corpus. Paying for an unmeasured component
is the same error as reporting an unmeasured number. Turn it on when the
ablation says it earns its place; `instance_type` and `enable_rerank` are both
variables, so that is a one-line change.

**Verified.** The image builds at 1.16 GB, runs, loads the embedder with no
network, connects to Postgres and serves the frontend:

```
{"status": "degraded", "checks": {"api_key_configured": false,
 "embedder_loaded": true, "llm_ready": false, "database": "ok"}}
```

---

## 0035 — A single static page, not Streamlit

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 6

**Context.** The brief offers "a single HTML page or Streamlit" for a frontend
showing the answer, clickable citations, latency and cost.

**Options.** Streamlit, or one static page served by the existing FastAPI app.

**Choice.** One self-contained HTML file with vanilla JavaScript, served at
`/`, with no build step and no CDN fetch.

**Why.** Streamlit is a dependency outside the agreed stack, a second process
and a second port, and it would double the deployment surface for a page with
one input and one result. The static page costs nothing extra: it ships inside
the package, is served by a route that already exists, and is testable through
the same `TestClient` as everything else.

Two details worth keeping. Citations deep-link as `url#page=N`, so a reader
lands on the page of the PDF the quote came from rather than its first page.
And abstention renders as a distinct state with its own styling, not as an
empty answer — a system whose selling point is declining to guess should make
declining look deliberate.

A missing page returns a short message rather than a 500, so a packaging slip
degrades the demo instead of looking like a total outage.

---

## 0036 — What the infrastructure deliberately leaves out

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 6

**Context.** The brief asks for free-tier-eligible options where possible. The
conventional AWS shapes for each component are not the cheap ones.

**Choice and why, item by item.**

*No NAT gateway* (~$32/month, more than everything else combined). The private
subnets hold only the database, which has no reason to reach the internet.

*No load balancer* (~$18/month). The instance serves port 80 directly behind a
CIDR allowlist. This means no TLS, which is recorded as a limitation rather
than hidden: widening `allowed_http_cidrs` to the world without adding TLS and
authentication would expose an endpoint that spends money per request.

*No Fargate* (~$26/month and no free tier). EC2 `t3.micro` is free for 750
h/month in the first year and fits the measured 242 MB footprint.

*SSM Parameter Store, not Secrets Manager* ($0 against $0.40 per secret per
month) — functionally equivalent for two values read at boot.

*No storage autoscaling on RDS.* `max_allocated_storage = 0`, because storage
that grows on its own is a bill that grows on its own.

*A cost budget with forecast alerts.* Two budgets per account are free.
Thresholds at 50/80/100% of actual plus a forecast alert, so a runaway shows
up on day three rather than day thirty. The SNS email subscription needs
confirming by hand; until then no alert is delivered, which the deployment
guide calls out as the silent failure it is.

**IAM.** The instance role can read objects in its own bucket and its own two
parameters, and decrypt only via `ssm.<region>.amazonaws.com`. No `rds:*` at
all — the database is reached with a password over the network, so the role
needs no database permission.

**Teardown.** `terraform destroy` leaves billable things behind, so the guide
walks through them: S3 object *versions* (versioning is on, so deleting
objects is not enough), the RDS final snapshot that destroy *creates* on its
way out, ECR images (~1.2 GB, not Terraform-managed), orphaned Elastic IPs,
and CloudWatch log groups.

**Validated, never applied.** `terraform fmt`, `terraform init -backend=false`
and `terraform validate` all pass against AWS provider ~> 5.70. No AWS account
was touched: no `apply`, no `destroy`, no mutating CLI call.

---

## 0037 — The README's numbers are generated, not written

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 7

**Context.** Rule 1 says no metric appears in README or `results/` unless a
script in this repository produced it. For six phases that held because nobody
had a number to type. It would stop holding the first time someone had one.

**Options.** Keep relying on discipline; add a review checklist; or make the
section mechanically derived.

**Choice.** `uv run poe docs` regenerates the README's Results section from
`results/*.csv`, spliced between HTML comment markers, and the DECISIONS index
from its own entries. With `results/` empty it writes `TODO` and says what is
missing.

**Why.** A rule enforced by discipline fails on the day someone is in a hurry,
and that is exactly the day a plausible-looking number gets pasted in. Deriving
the section means a figure can only reach the README by being measured. The
same applies to the index: a hand-maintained index of 36 entries across 1,000
lines is an index that is quietly wrong.

`--check` fails instead of writing, so CI can catch a stale README without
rewriting the working tree.

**A bug this surfaced.** The first anchor implementation built its slug from
number and title separately, producing `#0001-postgres-...`. GitHub slugs the
*rendered* heading: it strips the em dash but keeps the spaces either side, and
turns each space into a hyphen, giving `#0001--postgres-...` with a double
hyphen. Every link in the generated index would have failed silently — a
renderer does not complain about an anchor that does not exist. There is now a
test asserting every `DECISIONS.md#...` link in the README and the architecture
doc resolves, plus one asserting the prose links at all, so the first test
cannot pass by matching nothing.

---

## 0038 — Long-form documentation lives in docs/, not the README

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 7

**Context.** The README had grown to 345 lines across 16 sections, covering
ingestion, retrieval, answering, evaluation, the CI gate, the frontend and
deployment at roughly equal depth.

**Options.** Keep one long README; split by audience.

**Choice.** The README carries what a reader decides from in two minutes —
what the project is, the two refusals that make it interesting, a compact
diagram, results, a quick start, the decisions that shaped it, and the
limitations. Everything longer moved to `docs/architecture.md` and
`docs/reproduce.md`.

**Why.** A README nobody finishes is a README nobody reads the limitations of,
and on this project the limitations are the most important section. The
reproduction runbook in particular needed room to mark the three steps that
need a human and say why each one cannot be automated.

`AGENTS.md`, which had been an untracked copy of `CLAUDE.md` frozen several
phases earlier and still describing finished work as "not started", became a
three-line pointer. One source of truth, and tools that look for the file by
convention still find their way.

---

## 0039 — What this project does not have

**Date:** 2026-10-30 · **Phase:** 7

**Context.** Every phase is built. None of it has been run against real RBI
documents.

**Choice.** Say so first, in the status block, before anything else.

**Why.** A portfolio project is read by people deciding whether its author can
be trusted with their codebase, and the fastest way to fail that is a README
that reads as finished when it is not. The honest framing is also the stronger
one: the system is complete, the measurements are not taken, and the
measurement apparatus is itself the most carefully built part.

What is missing, concretely: no downloaded corpus (PDF acquisition is manual
by design — entry 0008), no human-verified evaluation set (nothing automated
may verify one — rule 2), no abstention threshold (nothing has been measured to
tune it on), no judge calibration, and Terraform that validates but has never
been applied.

Four bugs found during the build are recorded in their own entries rather than
quietly fixed, because each one would have produced a confident, wrong result:
conjunctive FTS scoring 0.0 recall on answerable questions
([0031](#0031--postgres-full-text-search-matches-disjunctively)), a CI gate
that passed an inverted retriever
([0033](#0033--the-gate-checks-order-sensitive-metrics-not-recall5-alone)),
chunk-id gold labels that would have made the ablation uncomputable
([0026](#0026--gold-evidence-is-labelled-as-spans-not-as-chunk-ids)), and an
anchor slugger whose links all failed silently
([0037](#0037--the-readmes-numbers-are-generated-not-written)).
